data.instruction: Learn the three basic present simple patterns.
data.title: Present simple form

blocks.title: Positive
blocks.content: Use the base verb with I, you, we and they. Add -s or -es with he, she and it.
blocks.secondary: I work. She works.

blocks.title: Negative
blocks.content: Use do not or does not plus the base verb.
blocks.secondary: They do not work. He does not work.

blocks.title: Question
blocks.content: Use Do or Does, then the subject, then the base verb.
blocks.secondary: Do you work? Does she work?

data.question: Choose the correct sentence.
data.explanation: With he, she or it, the present simple verb normally ends in -s or -es.

data.question: Complete the sentence: Mina ___ coffee in the evening.
data.explanation: After doesn't, use the base verb: drink.

data.question: Choose the correct question.
data.explanation: Use Does with your brother, followed by the base verb live.

data.instruction: Complete each sentence with the present simple form.
data.content: I {{work}} from home. Sara {{studies}} English. Leo {{watches}} the news and {{goes}} to bed early. We {{do_not_need}} a car. {{does_he_walk}} to college?

data.instruction: Correct both verb-form errors.
data.original: She don't drives to work.
answers: She does not drive to work.

data.title: You can build present simple statements and questions
data.subtitle: Next, connect the form to its main uses.

data.instruction: Connect repeated actions with the present simple.
data.title: Regular habits and repeated actions

blocks.title: Frequency words
blocks.content: Use the present simple with words such as always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely and never.
blocks.secondary: I usually walk to work.

blocks.title: Time expressions
blocks.content: Expressions such as every day, most mornings and on Fridays also show repetition.
blocks.secondary: We practise every evening.

blocks.title: Word position
blocks.content: Frequency adverbs normally go before a main verb but after the verb be.
blocks.secondary: She often cooks. She is often busy.

data.instruction: Classify each time phrase.

data.question: Choose the natural sentence.

options.label: I check usually my email after breakfast.
I usually check my email after breakfast.
I am usually check my email after breakfast.

data.explanation: Usually goes before the main verb check.

data.instruction: Use the present simple form.
data.content: Nora {{gets_up}} early most days. Her classes {{start}} at nine. She {{does_not_study}} on Sunday, and she {{is}} usually free that day.

data.instruction: Use these exact words to make a present simple sentence: Tom / play / football / every Saturday.
data.original: Tom's normal Saturday activity is football.

data.title: You can describe routines clearly
data.subtitle: Next, separate permanent situations, facts and duration.

data.instruction: Learn three important present-time meanings.
data.title: Permanent, factual, or continuing since the past?

blocks.title: Permanent situation
blocks.content: Use the present simple for a situation presented as stable or permanent.
blocks.secondary: My aunt owns a bakery.

blocks.title: Fact or general truth
blocks.content: Use the present simple for facts and generally accepted truths. General statements often use generally, mainly, normally, usually or traditionally.
blocks.secondary: Water boils at 100°C.

blocks.title: Duration up to now
blocks.content: Do not use the present simple to say how long a situation has continued from the past until now. Use the present perfect.
blocks.secondary: I have lived here since 2022.

data.instruction: Choose the meaning of each sentence.

items.label: The Earth moves around the Sun.
My parents teach at a college.

data.instruction: Use each word once: generally, mainly, normally, usually, traditionally.
data.content: {{traditionally}}, families celebrate this festival in spring. The museum {{normally}} opens at nine. People {{generally}} need sleep every night. This course {{mainly}} uses short examples. The journey {{usually}} takes two hours.

data.question: Choose the correct sentence about a situation that began in 2021 and is still true.
data.explanation: Use the present perfect for duration from a past starting point to now.

data.instruction: Complete the facts and permanent situations.
data.content: The library {{opens}} at eight. My cousin {{lives}} in Ankara. Ice {{melts}} when it gets warm. This machine {{uses}} very little power.

data.instruction: Complete with a present perfect form.
data.content: We {{have_lived}} in this house for six years.

data.title: You can distinguish facts, permanent situations and duration
data.subtitle: Next, use the present simple for instructions and stories.

data.instruction: Learn two less obvious uses of the present simple.
data.title: Steps and stories

blocks.title: Instructions and directions
blocks.content: Use the present simple to explain steps or directions.
blocks.secondary: First you open the file. Then you choose Save.

blocks.title: Stories and reviews
blocks.content: Use the present simple to tell the events of a story or describe what happens in a film, book or play.
blocks.secondary: The hero finds the key and escapes.

data.instruction: Classify each present simple use.

items.label: You turn right after the bank.
Next, you click the blue button.
At the end, the hero returns home.
In the film, two friends open a café.
I walk to class every day.

data.question: Which sentence is the clearest instruction?

options.label: First, you are entering your password.

data.explanation: Use the present simple for a sequence of instructions.

data.instruction: Complete the short process description.
data.content: First, the user {{opens}} the app. Next, the app {{asks}} for a password. The user {{types}} it and {{presses}} Continue.

data.instruction: Correct the tense in the film description.
data.original: In the final scene, the detective is finding the missing letter and solves the case.
answers: In the final scene, the detective finds the missing letter and solves the case.

data.title: You can use the present simple for steps and stories
data.subtitle: Next, build the present continuous accurately.

data.instruction: Learn the complete present continuous form.
data.title: Be plus verb-ing

blocks.title: Positive
blocks.content: Use am, is or are plus the -ing form.
blocks.secondary: I am working. She is working. They are working.

blocks.title: Negative
blocks.content: Put not after am, is or are.
blocks.secondary: He is not working. We are not working.

blocks.title: Question
blocks.content: Put am, is or are before the subject.
blocks.secondary: Are you working? Is she working?

data.question: Complete the sentence: The children ___ outside now.
data.explanation: Use are with the plural subject children.

data.question: Choose the correct negative sentence.
data.explanation: The negative is am not plus verb-ing.

data.question: Choose the correct question.
data.explanation: In a question, are comes before the subject you.

data.instruction: Complete each present continuous form.
data.content: I {{am_waiting}} for the bus. Mia {{is_studying}}. We {{are_not_using}} the room. {{are_they_coming}} with us?

data.instruction: Correct the verb form.
data.original: She is writeing an email.

data.title: You can build present continuous forms
data.subtitle: Next, choose it for actions now and temporary situations.

data.instruction: Connect present continuous forms with two core meanings.
data.title: Now or temporary

blocks.title: At the moment of speaking
blocks.content: Use the present continuous for an action happening now.
blocks.secondary: I am waiting outside.

blocks.title: Temporary situation
blocks.content: Use it for a situation around now that is not presented as permanent.
blocks.secondary: I am staying with my aunt this month.

blocks.title: Common signals
blocks.content: At the moment, currently, now and this week, month or year often point to a current or temporary situation.

data.instruction: Choose the meaning of each present continuous sentence.

items.label: Someone is knocking at the door.
I am taking an evening class this month.
We are working in Berlin for a short project.

data.question: Omar normally lives in Cairo, but this month he ___ in Dubai.
data.explanation: This month marks a temporary situation.

data.instruction: Use the present continuous.
data.content: Please be quiet; the baby {{is_sleeping}}. I {{am_using}} my brother's laptop this week. Our neighbours {{are_repairing}} their kitchen at the moment.

data.instruction: Correct the temporary situation.
data.original: I work at the city office this week because my usual office is closed.
answers: I am working at the city office this week because my usual office is closed.
I'm working at the city office this week because my usual office is closed.

data.title: You can describe actions now and temporary situations
data.subtitle: Next, use the continuous for change and trends.

data.instruction: Recognize change over time.
data.title: A situation that is developing

blocks.title: Trend or change
blocks.content: Use the present continuous when a situation is changing or developing around the present time.
blocks.secondary: Prices are rising. Online study is becoming more common.

blocks.title: Not every fact is a trend
blocks.content: Use the present simple for a stable fact. Use the continuous only when the sentence presents an ongoing change.

data.instruction: Separate stable facts from current trends.

data.question: The chart shows that demand ___ quickly this year.
data.explanation: The sentence describes a developing trend this year.

data.instruction: Complete the changing situations.
data.content: The town {{is_growing}} rapidly. More families {{are_moving}} here, and new shops {{are_opening}} every month.

data.instruction: Correct the trend sentence.
data.original: The cost of food goes up rapidly at the moment.
answers: The cost of food is going up rapidly at the moment.

data.title: You can describe current change
data.subtitle: Next, learn the emotional use of always with the continuous.

config.title: Always: neutral habit or emotional comment

data.instruction: Notice how the tense changes the speaker's attitude.
data.title: Two meanings with always

blocks.title: Neutral repeated fact
blocks.content: Use the present simple when always only reports a regular habit.
blocks.secondary: He always arrives at eight.

blocks.title: Complaint, surprise or envy
blocks.content: Use always, constantly, continually or forever with the present continuous to show that something happens more than expected and the speaker feels strongly about it.
blocks.secondary: He is always losing his keys!

data.instruction: Classify the speaker's meaning.

items.label: The bus always leaves at six.
They're always travelling to amazing places!
He is forever borrowing my charger!

data.question: Choose the sentence that clearly sounds like a complaint.

options.label: Sam always puts his cup here.
Sam is always leaving dirty cups on my desk!

data.explanation: Is always leaving presents the repeated action as annoying.

data.instruction: Use the form that matches the speaker's attitude.
data.content: Our class {{always_starts}} at nine; that is the timetable. But Lee {{is_always_arriving}} late, Nina {{is_continually_interrupting}} me, and Max {{is_forever_borrowing}} my notes!

data.instruction: Rewrite the sentence to make the annoyance explicit with the present continuous.
data.original: My neighbour constantly plays loud music at night!
acceptedAnswers: My neighbour is constantly playing loud music at night!
My neighbour's constantly playing loud music at night!
data.modelAnswer: My neighbour is constantly playing loud music at night!

data.title: You can distinguish neutral habits from emotional repetition
data.subtitle: Next, choose between both present tenses in mixed contexts.

data.instruction: Use meaning before looking at the time phrase.
data.title: A simple decision

blocks.title: Choose present simple
blocks.content: Ask whether the sentence is a habit, permanent situation, fact, instruction or story description.

blocks.title: Choose present continuous
blocks.content: Ask whether it is happening now, temporary, changing, or an emotional repeated action.

blocks.title: Check state verbs
blocks.content: A state verb normally stays in a simple form even when the state is true now.

data.instruction: Choose the tense required by each meaning.

data.question: I usually ___ at home, but today I ___ in the library.
data.explanation: Usually marks a habit; today marks the temporary contrast.

data.question: Choose the correct pair: The museum ___ at ten. Look, the guide ___ the door now.
data.explanation: The timetable is present simple; the action now is present continuous.

data.instruction: Choose the form from meaning.
data.content: Ben normally {{cycles}} to work, but he {{is_taking}} the bus this week. The bus {{leaves}} at 7:30, and more people {{are_using}} it because fuel prices {{are_rising}}.

data.instruction: Correct both tense choices.
data.original: I am usually walking to class, but today I walk with my friend.
answers: I usually walk to class, but today I am walking with my friend.
I usually walk to class, but today I'm walking with my friend.

data.title: You can choose the tense from context
data.subtitle: Next, learn which verbs normally describe states.

data.instruction: Group state verbs by the kind of state they describe.
data.title: State verbs normally use simple forms

blocks.title: Thoughts
blocks.content: Examples include agree, assume, believe, disagree, forget, hope, know, regret, remember, suppose, think and understand.

blocks.title: Feelings
blocks.content: Examples include adore, despise, dislike, enjoy, feel, hate, like, love, mind, prefer and want.

blocks.title: Senses
blocks.content: Examples include feel, hear, see, smell and taste.

blocks.title: Possession
blocks.content: Examples include have, own and belong.

blocks.title: Description
blocks.content: Examples include appear, contain, look, look like, mean, resemble, seem, smell, sound, taste and weigh.

data.instruction: Match each state-verb group to examples.
Classify each verb by its main state meaning.

data.question: Which sentence uses a state verb correctly?
data.explanation: Know describes a mental state and is not normally continuous.

data.instruction: Classify more state verbs from Unit 1.
Use simple forms for these states.
data.content: I {{understand}} the question. Maya {{prefers}} tea. This bag {{belongs}} to me. The box {{contains}} old photos.

data.title: You can recognize the main state-verb groups
data.subtitle: Next, apply the state-verb rule and its sense exception.

data.instruction: Avoid a common present continuous error.
data.title: A state can be true now without a continuous form

blocks.title: Normal rule
blocks.content: Do not normally use state verbs in the present continuous because they describe a state rather than a temporary activity.
blocks.secondary: I want some water. Not: I am wanting some water.

blocks.title: A current sense
blocks.content: To describe something you notice through a sense now, can is often natural.
blocks.secondary: I can hear music. I can smell smoke.

data.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.label: I am wanting to ask a question.
I want to ask a question.
I wanting to ask a question.

data.explanation: Want is normally a state verb.

data.question: There may be a fire. I ___ smoke.
data.explanation: Can smell is natural for a sense you notice now.

data.instruction: Complete the state sentences.
data.content: I {{believe}} you. This soup {{smells}} good. We {{own}} the flat. From here, I {{can_see}} the station.

data.instruction: Correct both state-verb errors.
data.original: I am knowing this word, but I am not understanding its meaning.
answers: I know this word, but I do not understand its meaning.
I know this word, but I don't understand its meaning.

data.title: You can keep ordinary states out of the continuous
data.subtitle: Next, learn when think, taste and have change meaning.

data.instruction: Choose the tense from the verb's meaning.
data.title: Some state verbs can describe temporary activities

blocks.title: think
blocks.content: Think is simple for an opinion, but continuous for the mental activity happening now.
blocks.secondary: I think it is useful. I am thinking about the problem.

blocks.title: taste
blocks.content: Taste is simple for a flavour, but continuous for the action of testing food.
blocks.secondary: The sauce tastes good. I am tasting the sauce.

blocks.title: have
blocks.content: Have is simple for possession, but continuous for an experience or activity.
blocks.secondary: I have a bicycle. We are having lunch.

data.instruction: Match each form to its meaning.

data.question: Choose the correct pair: I ___ this plan is good, but I ___ about one possible problem.
data.explanation: The first is an opinion; the second is mental activity now.

data.question: Choose the correct pair: The soup ___ salty, so the cook ___ it again.
data.explanation: Tastes describes flavour; is tasting describes the cook's action.

data.question: Choose the correct pair: We ___ a small garden, and we ___ a picnic there now.
data.explanation: Have is possession; are having is a current activity.

data.instruction: Choose each form from its meaning.
data.content: I {{think}} this tea is excellent. The waiter {{is_tasting}} a new dessert. We {{have}} two tickets, and we {{are_having}} a great time.

data.instruction: Correct both meanings of have.
data.original: I am having a new laptop, and I have lunch with my team right now.
answers: I have a new laptop, and I am having lunch with my team right now.
I have a new laptop, and I'm having lunch with my team right now.

data.title: You can choose forms for think, taste and have
data.subtitle: Next, repair mixed present-tense errors.

data.instruction: Use the same three checks for every sentence.
data.title: Check meaning, helper and verb form

blocks.title: 1. Meaning
blocks.content: Decide whether the sentence describes a simple-present meaning or a continuous-present meaning.

blocks.title: 2. Helper
blocks.content: Check do or does for present simple negatives and questions, and am, is or are for the continuous.

blocks.title: 3. Main verb
blocks.content: Use the base verb after do or does, and the -ing form after am, is or are.
